section.title: The Lampstand, the Bread, and the Blasphemer
section.sectionRationale: This chapter pauses the festival calendar to give two ongoing tabernacle duties, the lampstand oil and the bread of the Presence, and then narrates a specific case of blasphemy that establishes equal justice for native Israelite and foreigner alike.
section.thesis: Between Israel's appointed feasts, God maintains a continual light and a continual bread before Him in the tabernacle, and when a man blasphemes His name, He establishes through a real case that His name must be honored and that the same standard of justice applies to native and foreigner alike.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the continual lamp, tended by Aaron every evening; the bread of the Presence, set out weekly and eaten by the priests; and the narrative of the blasphemer, leading to the law of exact retribution, applied equally to all.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Command the Israelites to bring you pure oil of pressed olives for the light, to keep the {{ner|lamps}} burning continually.

Outside the veil of the Testimony in the Tent of Meeting, Aaron is to tend the lamps continually before the LORD from evening until morning. This is to be a permanent statute for the generations to come.
He shall tend the lamps on the pure gold lampstand before the LORD continually.
You are also to take fine flour and bake twelve loaves, using two-tenths of an ephah for each loaf,
and set them in two rows, six per row, on the {{panim|table of pure gold before the LORD}}.
And you are to place pure frankincense near each row, so that it may serve as a memorial portion for the bread, an offering made by fire to the LORD.
Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant.
It belongs to Aaron and his sons, who are to eat it in a holy place; for it is to him a most holy part of the offerings made by fire to the LORD, his portion forever.”

units.label: The blasphemer
units.note: a real case brought to Moses

verses.text: Now the son of an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father went out among the Israelites, and a fight broke out in the camp between him and an Israelite.
The son of the Israelite woman blasphemed the {{shem|Name}} with a curse. So they brought him to Moses. (His mother’s name was Shelomith daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan.)
They placed him in custody until the will of the LORD should be made clear to them.
Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Take the blasphemer outside the camp, and have all who heard him lay their hands on his head; then have the whole assembly stone him.
And you are to tell the Israelites, ‘If anyone curses his God, he shall bear the consequences of his sin.

Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD must surely be put to death; the whole assembly must surely stone him, whether he is a foreign resident or native; if he blasphemes the Name, he must be put to death.

units.label: Life for life, one law for all

verses.text: And if a man takes the life of anyone else, he must surely be put to death.
Whoever kills an animal must make restitution, life for life.
If anyone injures his neighbor, whatever he has done must be done to him:
fracture {{tachat|for}} fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth. Just as he injured the other person, the same must be inflicted on him.
Whoever kills an animal must make restitution, but whoever kills a man must be put to death.
You are to have the same standard of law for the foreign resident and the native; for I am the LORD your God.’”
Then Moses spoke to the Israelites, and they took the blasphemer outside the camp and stoned him. So the Israelites did as the LORD had commanded Moses.

ner.gloss: The continual lamp, tended nightly so its light never failed. Its unbroken burning before the LORD becomes, in the New Testament, a picture fulfilled in Christ, the light of the world, and in the church, His lampstand, called to shine without ceasing.

panim.gloss: Literally bread of the face or presence, twelve loaves representing Israel's tribes kept continually before God on the golden table. Their unbroken presence pictures a people kept perpetually in fellowship with God, later fulfilled in Christ, the bread of life.

shem.gloss: The Name, used here as a reverent way of referring to the LORD Himself. Blaspheming the Name treats God's own character and reputation with contempt, which is why this single case receives such careful, direct divine instruction.

tachat.gloss: In place of, instead of, or for. This small preposition structures the whole formula of exact retribution, fracture for fracture, eye for eye, establishing a judicial standard of proportional, not excessive, justice for the courts to administer.

basic.context: This chapter interrupts the festival calendar to describe two ongoing tabernacle duties, tending the continual lamp and setting out the weekly bread before the LORD, then tells the story of a man who blasphemed God's name, resulting in a law of exact justice applied equally to native and foreigner.
basic.hermeneutics: The tabernacle furniture and rituals here belong to old covenant ceremonial law fulfilled in Christ; the blasphemer's civil penalty belonged to Israel's specific old covenant order. The enduring principle, reverence for God's name and impartial justice, continues to bind God's people today, even where the specific penalties do not.
basic.originalLanguages: The ner tamid, continual lamp, and the lechem panim, bread of the presence, both picture something kept perpetually before God without lapse. Shem, the Name, names God's own reputation as what the blasphemer defiled. Tachat, in place of, structures the eye for eye formula as a judicial limiting principle, not a license for private revenge.
basic.typology: The continually burning lamp anticipates Christ, the light of the world, and His church as a lampstand; the continually present bread anticipates Christ, the bread of life, who keeps His people perpetually in God's presence.
basic.christ: Jesus says, I am the light of the world, John 8:12, and I am the bread of life, John 6:35, fulfilling in Himself both objects this chapter requires to burn and be set out without fail. Where Israel's lamp and bread had to be constantly tended by human hands, Christ Himself is the unfailing light and sustenance His people now depend on.
basic.god: God cares about the small, repeated tasks of worship, nightly oil, weekly bread, as much as the grand annual feasts, and when His own name is blasphemed, He requires the whole community to take it with the utmost seriousness, while insisting the same law govern native and foreigner alike.
basic.crossReferences: John 8:12 calls Christ the light of the world. John 6:35 calls Him the bread of life. Matthew 5:38-39 addresses the popular misuse of eye for eye as personal license for revenge. Numbers 15:16 echoes this chapter's insistence on one law for native and foreigner.
basic.oneStory: God's unbroken light and bread before Him in the tabernacle, and His insistence on impartial justice for native and foreigner alike, both anticipate the completeness of what Christ provides: an unfailing light and life for His people, and a perfect justice satisfied fully and finally at the cross.

context.literary:
Chapter 23 laid out Israel's year: Sabbath, Passover, Firstfruits, Weeks, Trumpets, the Day of Atonement and Booths. Chapter 24 then shrinks the scale of time. The lamps are tended 'from evening until morning,' verse 3, a nightly rhythm, and the bread is renewed 'every Sabbath day,' verse 8, a weekly one. Read together, chapters 23 and 24 give Israel the whole architecture of sacred time, annual, weekly and daily, before chapter 25 stretches it out to seven years and fifty.

The chapter falls into two halves that look unrelated at first. Verses 1 to 9 are instruction for the Holy Place; verses 10 to 23 are one of only two stretches of narrative in Leviticus, the other being the ordination and the death of Nadab and Abihu in chapters 8 to 10. Both stories concern the holiness of God being treated lightly, and both end in death. The narrative is framed by an inclusio: 'Take the blasphemer outside the camp,' verse 14, and 'they took the blasphemer outside the camp and stoned him,' verse 23.

Inside that frame the ruling of verses 16 to 22 is arranged concentrically. It opens and closes with the insistence on one law for foreigner and native, verses 16 and 22. Next come the killing of a man, verses 17 and 21b, then the killing of an animal, verses 18 and 21a, and at the centre sits the injury law, 'fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth,' verse 20. The shape itself teaches: the formula of equal measure stands at the heart of a unit bracketed by equal law for every person.

The link between the halves is the phrase 'before the LORD.' The lamp burns before Him, the bread lies before Him, and the blasphemer's crime is committed against the Name of the One whose presence the lamp and bread honour.
context.historical:
The lampstand stood in the Holy Place on the south side, opposite the table on the north, Exodus 40:22-24, just 'outside the veil of the Testimony,' verse 3, the curtain that screened the ark holding the stone tablets. Its oil was 'pure oil of pressed olives,' olives crushed by hand so that the first, clearest oil ran off without heat or heavy pressing, the kind that burns with little smoke. Here the people supply it: 'Command the Israelites to bring you' the oil, verse 2. The priest tends the flame, but every household has a share in keeping God's house lit.

The loaves were large. The BSB footnote to verse 5 reckons two tenths of an ephah at about four dry quarts, some two kilograms of flour to each loaf, twelve loaves for the twelve tribes. Frankincense lay beside each row and was burned as the memorial portion, verse 7, when the bread was removed and eaten by the priests. The practice is visible centuries later at Nob, where the old bread had been 'replaced with hot bread on the day it was taken away,' 1 Samuel 21:6, and in Abijah's boast that Judah still set out 'the rows of showbread' and lit the lamps 'every evening,' 2 Chronicles 13:11.

The blasphemer belonged to the 'mixed multitude' that came out of Egypt with Israel, Exodus 12:38. His mother is named, Shelomith daughter of Dibri of Dan, which fixes the event in a real family and a real tribe. When the case arose Moses did not improvise. As with the Sabbath wood gatherer, Numbers 15:34, the man was held in custody until the LORD gave a ruling. Stoning by the whole congregation made the verdict communal, and requiring those who heard the curse to lay hands on his head first placed responsibility on the witnesses, as Deuteronomy 17:7 later requires.

In the wider world, law codes such as Hammurabi's used the principle of equal measure but scaled penalties by the social class of the victim and the offender. Israel's ruling here explicitly refuses that kind of sliding scale.
context.canonical:
The lamp and bread first appear as commands in Exodus, where the oil is required in almost identical words, Exodus 27:20-21, and the table holds 'the Bread of the Presence ... before Me at all times,' Exodus 25:30. Leviticus 24 turns furniture into ongoing practice. Later history shows the lamp still burning in Samuel's boyhood, 'before the lamp of God had gone out,' 1 Samuel 3:3, a phrase that also hints at how dim Israel's spiritual life had become. Zechariah sees a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees and hears, 'Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit,' Zechariah 4:2-6, so the lamp becomes a picture of God's people kept alight by His Spirit.

The bread reappears when David and his men eat it at Nob, 1 Samuel 21:6, and Jesus cites that very episode to show that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath, Matthew 12:3-4. Hebrews lists 'the lampstand, the table, and the consecrated bread' as the furnishings of the first room of the tabernacle, Hebrews 9:2, before showing how Christ has entered the true sanctuary.

The blasphemy law stands behind several of Scripture's darkest scenes. Jezebel manufactures the charge that Naboth 'cursed both God and the king,' and he is taken 'outside the city and stoned,' 1 Kings 21:13. Stephen is dragged out of the city and stoned after false witnesses accuse him of blasphemy, Acts 6:11 and 7:58. Jesus Himself is charged with blasphemy, Mark 14:64, is threatened with stones for it, John 10:33, and suffers 'outside the city gate,' Hebrews 13:12. The injury formula of verse 20 is repeated in Exodus 21:23-25 and Deuteronomy 19:21, and is quoted by Jesus in Matthew 5:38, as the BSB footnote notes.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see that God's presence among them was sustained by faithful, ordinary, repeated obedience. Oil had to be brought, wicks trimmed each evening, bread baked each week. No single great act kept the sanctuary lit and supplied; a whole people's steady giving did. The lamp and the bread said, night after night and week after week, that Israel stood before the LORD and that He kept them in view.

The narrative then shows what it means to despise that presence. A man in a quarrel uses the Name as a weapon. Moses wanted Israel to grasp that God's name is not a word to be thrown in a fight, and that treating it lightly is not a private matter but an offence the whole community must answer for, since the whole community lives under that Name.

He also wanted them to learn how justice works in a holy nation. The case of a man with an Egyptian father could have been settled by prejudice, harshly or leniently. Instead God rules that the same law binds 'the foreign resident and the native,' verse 22, and that punishment must match the wrong, no more and no less. The closing sentence, 'So the Israelites did as the LORD had commanded Moses,' verse 23, holds up an obedient community as the model.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Three kinds of material sit side by side. The lamp and bread are prescribed ritual, called 'a permanent statute,' verse 3, for as long as the tabernacle order stood; Hebrews 9:2-10 treats that order as a copy pointing to Christ, so the church keeps no lamp or table but learns what they meant. The story of verses 10 to 12 and 23 is description: it records one case and one execution. Verses 15 to 22 are the ruling that came out of it, genuine law for Israel as a civil and religious nation.

Christians are not a theocratic state and do not execute blasphemers; the New Testament gives the church the discipline of the word and of fellowship, not the sword. Yet what the ruling protects still stands. God's name is to be hallowed, Matthew 6:9, and the tongue that curses is condemned, James 3:9-10. Proportional, impartial justice remains the calling of civil authority, Romans 13:4, while personal vengeance is forbidden to believers, Romans 12:19.

debates.question: Does the lex talionis, eye for eye, in verses 19-20 endorse personal revenge?

views.label: A judicial limiting principle, not a license for private revenge
views.case: Most interpreters read this as instruction to courts, limiting punishment to proportional, not excessive, retribution, guarding against escalating blood feuds, not authorizing individuals to take justice into their own hands.

views.label: Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:38-39 as a deliberate contrast
views.case: Some see Jesus specifically addressing a popular misuse of this principle as personal license for retaliation, redirecting His followers from personal vengeance toward active nonresistance and love of enemies, without thereby abolishing the state's proper administration of justice, addressed in Romans 13:4.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the text is a judicial standard for courts, not a license for private revenge, and that Jesus' teaching addresses personal conduct between individuals, not the legitimate role of courts and civil authority in administering proportional justice.

debates.question: What exactly was the blasphemer's crime: cursing God, or pronouncing the divine name?

views.label: Cursing God by His name
views.case: Verse 11 pairs two verbs: he 'blasphemed the Name with a curse,' and verse 15 speaks of anyone who 'curses his God.' The offence is using God's name to call down harm or to revile Him, in the heat of a fight, which is the sin prohibited in Exodus 22:28. On this reading the name is not dangerous to speak; it is dangerous to degrade.

views.label: Pronouncing the Name in a forbidden way
views.case: The verb in verses 11 and 16 can mean to designate or specify by name, as in Numbers 1:17, and the ancient Greek translation rendered verse 16 as naming the name of the Lord. Later Jewish practice of avoiding the pronunciation of the divine name, and of speaking instead of 'the Name,' grew partly from this reading, treating any casual utterance as a step toward profanation.

debates.bearing: The immediate context favours the first view, since the man cursed during a quarrel and verse 15 speaks of cursing. The reverence behind the second view is right, but Scripture itself invites God's people to call on His name, Exodus 3:15, and Jesus taught them to hallow it, Matthew 6:9, not to leave it unspoken.

study.originalLanguages:
Tamid, 'continually,' governs the first half of the chapter, repeated in verses 2, 3 and 4. It does not mean that the flame never went out. Verse 3 limits the tending to 'from evening until morning,' and 1 Samuel 3:3 assumes the lamp could go out before dawn. Tamid means regular and unfailing, as in the 'regular burnt offering' offered morning and evening, Exodus 29:42 and Numbers 28:3. What God asks is not a spectacular flame but a faithful rhythm that is never skipped.

The verb for tending the lamps and setting out the bread, arak, runs through verses 3, 4 and 8. It means to set in order or arrange, the verb used of the priests who 'arrange wood on the fire,' Leviticus 1:7, and of Moses who 'arranged the bread' on the table, Exodus 40:23. Worship in the Holy Place was an ordered, careful thing, done in rows and at set times, not left to impulse.

The frankincense in verse 7 serves as the azkarah, 'memorial portion,' from zakar, to remember. The same term names the handful of grain offering burned on the altar, Leviticus 2:2. Burned as the bread is removed, it rises as a reminder before God that the twelve tribes are His and are in His presence. The bread is set out 'on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant,' berit olam, verse 8, the phrase used of God's everlasting covenant with Abraham, Genesis 17:7.

The crime in verse 11 is described with two verbs. Naqab has a basic sense of piercing, as a reed 'will pierce the hand,' 2 Kings 18:21, and a further sense of designating by name, Numbers 1:17. Qalal, 'curse,' verses 11, 14, 15 and 23, comes from a root meaning to be light or slight, the opposite of kabad, to be heavy, which gives the word for glory. To curse God is to treat as weightless the One whose glory is weightiest. The two roots meet in 1 Samuel 2:30: 'I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained.'

The penalty in verse 15 is that he 'shall bear the consequences of his sin,' literally shall carry his sin, nasa chet. The same verb is used when the goat carries Israel's iniquities, Leviticus 16:22. Guilt is a burden that someone must carry. Finally, 'the same standard of law' in verse 22 is literally 'one judgment,' mishpat echad, the same idea as Exodus 12:49 and Numbers 15:29.

typology.type: The lamp tended every evening before the LORD, Leviticus 24:2-4
typology.fulfillment: The lamp gave the only light in a windowless room where the priest served beside the table and the incense altar. Christ says, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12, and John calls Him the light that 'shines in the darkness,' John 1:5. The escalation is that His people are made lamps too: 'You are the light of the world,' Matthew 5:14, and the churches are 'seven golden lampstands' among which Christ walks, Revelation 1:20. The type falls short because it needed nightly oil from human hands; the new Jerusalem needs no lamp at all, for 'the Lamb is its lamp,' Revelation 21:23.

typology.type: Twelve loaves arranged before the LORD each Sabbath, Leviticus 24:5-9
typology.fulfillment: The loaves represented all twelve tribes held continually before God's face, and they were eaten by priests in a holy place. Jesus calls Himself 'the living bread that came down from heaven,' John 6:51, and on the night He was betrayed He took bread and said, 'this is My body,' Matthew 26:26. The escalation is twofold: the bread is no longer reserved for Aaron's sons, since all believers are now a priesthood who eat, and the One pictured is not a people represented but the Son who represents them. The type falls short because the bread went stale weekly; Christ 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25.

typology.type: The blasphemer taken outside the camp and stoned, Leviticus 24:14, 23
typology.fulfillment: The pattern is a contrast rather than a simple likeness. Jesus was condemned as a blasphemer, Mark 14:64, and 'went out' carrying His cross, John 19:17, suffering 'outside the city gate,' Hebrews 13:12. The One who bore the penalty for dishonouring the Name was the One who had perfectly hallowed it, John 17:6. In Leviticus the guilty man bears his own sin, verse 15; at the cross the innocent bears the sin of others. The type falls short because the charge against Him was false; what He truly carried was our blasphemy, not His.

typology.type: One law for the native and the foreigner, Leviticus 24:22
typology.fulfillment: Israel's courts were to weigh an Egyptian's son with the same scales as a full Israelite. In Christ the equality moves from judgment to grace: 'There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus,' Galatians 3:28. The same law once condemned native and foreigner alike; now the same gospel welcomes both on the same terms. The type falls short because it guaranteed only equal justice, while the gospel offers equal mercy.

study.christ:
The first half of Leviticus 24 describes what the priest did in the Holy Place every day and every week: trim the lamps, arrange the bread, burn the memorial incense. The Gospel of John takes up both objects. 'I am the bread of life,' John 6:35, comes in the chapter that begins with Jesus feeding a multitude and recalling the manna. 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12, is spoken at the Feast of Booths, where, according to later Jewish tradition, great lamps were lit in the temple courts. Jesus presents Himself as the reality the tabernacle furniture only portrayed. The link is not forced allegory; John deliberately arranges these sayings around Israel's worship, and Hebrews 9:2 names lampstand and bread among the things that were 'a copy and shadow,' Hebrews 8:5.

There is a further step. The twelve loaves stood for Israel as a people held before God's face. In Christ the people are not merely represented by bread on a table; they are represented by a living High Priest who 'always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:25. What the priest did weekly, Christ does without ceasing.

The second half of the chapter leads to Christ by contrast. The only man stoned in Leviticus dies for cursing the Name. The Gospels record that Jesus was repeatedly accused of that very crime. The scribes said, 'He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?' Mark 2:7. When He said, 'before Abraham was born, I am,' they 'picked up stones to throw at Him,' John 8:58-59. At His trial the high priest tore his clothes and declared, 'He has blasphemed!' Matthew 26:65, and the council condemned Him 'as deserving of death,' Mark 14:64. The law of Leviticus 24 was, humanly speaking, the legal instrument of His death.

Yet the charge was the reverse of the truth. Jesus did not degrade the Name; He is the one to whom God 'gave the name above all names,' Philippians 2:9. He was taken outside, as the blasphemer was, and Hebrews draws the lesson: 'Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood,' Hebrews 13:12. The blasphemer bore his own sin; Christ bore ours. And where verse 20 required measured retaliation, He 'did not retaliate' but entrusted Himself 'to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23, praying for those who killed Him, Luke 23:34. The demands of exact justice were not waived; they were met in Him.
study.god:
Leviticus 24 shows a God who wants to be present and wants His presence to be honoured. He asks for a lamp that burns each night and bread that is renewed each week. The request is not for His benefit, as if He needed light or food; the lamp lit the room where priests served, and the bread was eaten by them. It is for Israel's benefit, a standing sign that they were before Him and He had not forgotten them. The memorial portion of frankincense, verse 7, was a reminder offered up to the God who, in Exodus 2:24, 'remembered His covenant.'

The chapter also shows the weight of God's name. The name is His self-revelation, what He has made known of Himself, Exodus 3:15. To curse Him by it is to take what He has given as a gift of relationship and use it as a weapon. The ruling in verse 16 is severe, and it should unsettle modern readers enough to ask what it reveals. It reveals that God is not a local deity whose honour matters only to Israel; His name is holy for 'the foreign resident' as much as for 'the native.' It echoes Leviticus 22:32, 'You must not profane My holy name.' It also shows that God is patient in the process: Moses waits, the man is held, the LORD speaks, and only then is judgment given. God's holiness is never capricious.

Then there is justice. God rules that a life taken requires a life, verse 17, because, as Genesis 9:6 explains, 'in His own image God has made mankind.' He distinguishes a man from an animal: killing a beast brings restitution, killing a person brings death, verse 21. He limits punishment to what fits the wrong, so that anger does not escalate into feud. He refuses to let status or ancestry tip the scales, verse 22. The phrase that seals it is 'for I am the LORD your God.' Impartial justice is not merely good policy; it is an expression of who God is.

The tension the chapter holds is between a God who draws near in light and bread, and a God before whom contempt is fatal. The New Testament does not dissolve the tension; it deepens it. 'Our God is a consuming fire,' Hebrews 12:29, and the same letter invites us to draw near with confidence. Worship that holds both is reverent and glad at once: it hallows the Name, Matthew 6:9, and comes daily for bread.

crossReferences.note: The original command for the lamp oil, in nearly identical wording: 'pure oil of pressed olives for the light,' tended 'from evening until morning' as 'a permanent statute.' Leviticus 24:2-4 repeats it as a standing duty now that the tabernacle is built, and lays the supply on the whole people.

The table is to hold 'the Bread of the Presence ... before Me at all times.' Leviticus 24:5-9 supplies what Exodus left open: twelve loaves, their size, their arrangement in two rows, the frankincense memorial, the weekly change on the Sabbath and the priests' right to eat them.

At Nob the priest gives David the consecrated bread, 'which had been removed from before the LORD and replaced with hot bread on the day it was taken away.' It shows the weekly rhythm of Leviticus 24:8 still kept, and raises the question Jesus later answers about need and holy things.

Jesus cites David eating 'the consecrated bread, which was not lawful for them to eat, but only for the priests,' a direct reference to Leviticus 24:9. He uses it to show that mercy and the presence of One greater than the temple outweigh a rigid reading of ritual law.

A close twin of this narrative. A man gathers wood on the Sabbath; he is brought to Moses, held in custody 'because it had not been declared what should be done,' then stoned outside the camp by the whole congregation. Both cases show how Israel's law grew from real situations brought before God.

'You must not blaspheme God or curse the ruler of your people.' The basic command stood in the Book of the Covenant; Leviticus 24:15-16 supplies its penalty and extends its reach explicitly to the foreign resident, so that no one living among Israel could curse God with impunity.

The first statement of the equal measure principle: 'a life for a life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth.' Verses 26 and 27 show that it could be satisfied by compensation, since a slave blinded by his master goes free 'as compensation for the eye.' This shapes how Leviticus 24:19-20 should be read.

Jesus quotes the formula of Leviticus 24:20 and tells His disciples 'not to resist an evil person.' He does not abolish public justice but forbids using a court principle as a warrant for personal retaliation, calling His followers to absorb insult rather than return it.

Naboth is falsely accused of having 'cursed both God and the king,' then 'taken outside the city and stoned.' The episode shows the blasphemy law of Leviticus 24 turned into a weapon by corrupt rulers, the danger of which is why Scripture insists on true witnesses, Deuteronomy 17:6.

The council hears Jesus confess Himself the Son of Man and condemns Him 'as deserving of death' for blasphemy. It is the law of Leviticus 24:16 applied to the one person in whom the Name was perfectly honoured, the gravest miscarriage of justice in history.

'Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood.' Like the blasphemer, He was taken outside the camp, verse 23, but to sanctify others rather than to bear His own guilt. Believers are called to go to Him there, 'bearing the disgrace He bore.'

The 'seven golden lampstands' are the seven churches, and the risen Christ walks among them. The lamp that Aaron tended before the LORD becomes the church itself, kept burning by the presence of its High Priest, who also warns that a lampstand can be removed.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God said, 'Let there be light,' and He set lights in the sky 'to mark the seasons and days and years,' Genesis 1:14. In the Holy Place Israel kept a small echo of that first creation: a lamp shining in darkness through each night and bread set out on each seventh day. The tabernacle was a portable Eden, and the lamp and table told Israel that God still meant to dwell with people and feed them in His presence, as He had in the garden.

The fall is present too. A man, in a quarrel with his brother, turns the Name of God into a curse. The camp is not Eden; sin reaches even into the community gathered around God's house, and death follows it. The story also looks back to Cain, whose quarrel with his brother ended in blood, and to God's word after the flood that a life taken demands a life, Genesis 9:6. Leviticus 24:17-22 is that word written into Israel's courts.

Redemption moves through both halves. The lamp and bread point forward to the One who is the light of the world and the bread of life. The blasphemy law points forward to the trial where the true Son was condemned under it and taken outside the camp to die. In that death the justice of 'life for life' is not set aside but fulfilled, as He gave His life for many.

The story ends where Revelation ends. The city needs no lampstand, for 'the Lamb is its lamp,' Revelation 21:23, and 'there will be no more night,' Revelation 22:5. There will be no curse, Revelation 22:3, and God's servants 'will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads,' Revelation 22:4. The Name once cursed in the camp will be worn with joy by every citizen, native and foreigner alike, gathered from every nation.

quiz.q: Who was responsible for tending the continual lamp, according to verses 3-4?

options.text: Aaron, tending it continually from evening until morning.
options.note: Verses 3-4 name Aaron specifically for this duty.

options.text: Any Israelite who happened to be near the tabernacle.
options.note: The text specifically assigns this duty to Aaron, not the general public.

options.text: The blasphemer named later in the chapter.
options.note: The chapter's structure separates the lamp instructions from the unrelated case of the blasphemer.

options.text: No one is assigned this duty.
options.note: Verses 3-4 explicitly assign this duty to Aaron.

quiz.q: How often was the bread on the golden table renewed, according to verse 8?

options.text: Every Sabbath day.
options.note: Verse 8 specifies this weekly renewal.

options.text: Once a year, on the Day of Atonement.
options.note: Verse 8 specifies a weekly, not yearly, renewal.

options.text: Every single day.
options.note: Verse 8 specifies weekly renewal, not daily.

options.text: No renewal schedule is given.
options.note: Verse 8 explicitly gives a weekly schedule.

quiz.q: What was the background of the man who blasphemed the Name in this chapter?

options.text: He was the son of an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father.
options.note: Verse 10 states this directly.

options.text: He was a fully native born Israelite priest.
options.note: Verse 10 specifically identifies his mixed parentage, not priestly status.

options.text: No information about him is given.
options.note: Verse 10 gives specific information about his parentage.

options.text: He was a foreign visitor with no connection to Israel.
options.note: Verse 10 identifies his mother as Israelite, giving him a direct connection to the community.

quiz.q: To whom did God say the law of blasphemy and the law of exact retribution should apply equally?

options.text: Both the foreign resident and the native-born Israelite.
options.note: Verses 16 and 22 both state this explicitly.

options.text: Only to native-born Israelites.
options.note: Verses 16 and 22 explicitly extend the law to foreigners as well.

options.text: Only to priests and Levites.
options.note: The text specifies native and foreigner broadly, not a priestly class specifically.

options.text: No specific group is named.
options.note: Verses 16 and 22 explicitly name both groups.

quiz.q: How does Jesus engage the principle of eye for eye in Matthew 5:38-39?

options.text: He addresses its popular misuse as personal license for revenge, calling His followers to active nonresistance instead.
options.note: Matthew 5:38-39 records this teaching directly.

options.text: He commands that courts abandon all standards of proportional justice.
options.note: Jesus addresses personal conduct between individuals, not the courts' legitimate administration of justice.

options.text: He has no teaching related to this principle.
options.note: Matthew 5:38-39 directly engages this principle.

options.text: He affirms personal revenge as the appropriate response to injury.
options.note: Jesus explicitly redirects His followers away from personal revenge in this teaching.

questions: The lamp and bread required faithful, repeated, often unnoticed maintenance. What unglamorous, repeated disciplines of your own faith need fresh faithfulness this week, even when no one is watching?

The blasphemer's case shows that how we speak of God matters enormously to Him. How careless or reverent is your own speech, whether about God directly or about matters of faith, when you are frustrated or provoked?
God insisted that the very same law govern native Israelite and foreign resident. Where might you be applying a double standard, harsher or more lenient, to people different from yourself?

Jesus is the light of the world and the bread of life, fulfilling what Israel's tabernacle furniture could only picture. Where do you look for light or sustenance apart from Him, and what would it look like to return to Him as your actual source?

The law of eye for eye limited punishment to what was proportional, not excessive. Where do you need to let go of a desire for revenge that exceeds the actual wrong done to you, trusting God's justice instead of taking it into your own hands?

translationNotes.note: Memorial portion translates a term describing the frankincense burned as a token representing the whole offering of bread before the LORD, similar to the memorial portion in grain offerings elsewhere in Leviticus.

Blasphemed the Name with a curse likely describes a specific, deliberate act of cursing using God's own covenant name, YHWH, rather than a vague or general expression of frustration, explaining the case's severity and the need for direct divine instruction.

Fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth is widely understood by both ancient and modern interpreters as a judicial ceiling limiting courts to proportional punishment, rather than a license authorizing private citizens to exact revenge themselves.
